title: Relational algebra: from questions to plans
lead: Transform one product table before reading a nested algebra expression.
goals: Evaluate relational operators on small datasets
Distinguish set projection from SQL bag projection
Turn a join question into an expression you can check

sections.title: Give each table transformation a name
sections.html:
SQL told us what answer to request. Now we need a language for the steps that compute it. Begin with an original product table:

R(pid, category)
11 tea
12 tea
13 cake

Ask for tea products. Examine each row: 11 is tea, 12 is tea, 13 is cake. Keep {(11,tea),(12,tea)}. The operation keeps rows satisfying a condition and leaves the columns pid,category intact. We call it selection, written σ category=tea(R). Read σ as “keep rows where”. It is not SQL's SELECT column list.

Ask instead for the categories present. Remove pid from each row: tea,tea,cake. In pure relational algebra, a relation is a set, so identical resulting rows collapse to {tea,cake}. This is projection, written π category(R): keep the named columns. It can preserve row count if all projected rows differ. SQL SELECT category normally keeps all three occurrences; SELECT DISTINCT category matches the set result.

Both outputs are relations: table-shaped values with a schema. We can therefore compose them: first select tea products, then project their category, giving {tea}. This property is closure. The schema still matters: σ price>25(R) is invalid because R has no price column. An invalid expression is not a valid query returning an empty relation.

Relational algebra names operations on relations; relational calculus expresses conditions defining a result. Their connection explains how a declarative question can be translated into operations. Codd-style equivalence concerns safe/domain-independent relational queries, not every unrestricted logical formula or all modern SQL features.

Try: project pid instead of category. Will three rows become two?

No: {11,12,13} has three distinct values. Projection removes duplicate output rows when they arise; it does not promise a smaller result every time.

Why can an RA operator feed another operator?

Its result is a relation, but the next operator must still use valid attributes and compatible schemas.

sections.title: Build a join by checking pairs
sections.html:
R has categories but no prices. Add an original second table:

S(pid, price)
11 20
13 35
14 50

To attach prices, first imagine every R row paired with every S row. With three rows in each table, there are 3×3=9 pairs. This is the Cartesian product, R × S. Most pairs associate different product IDs and are not useful matches. Inspect all nine ID pairs:

R.pidS.pid values paired with itEqual-ID pair kept
1111,13,14(11,tea,11,20)
1211,13,14None
1311,13,14(13,cake,13,35)

Filtering the product on R.pid=S.pid keeps two rows. Product followed by a condition is a theta join: R ⋈ R.pid=S.pid S. Equality conditions make it an equi-join. Its output columns are R.pid,category,S.pid,price; qualify or rename the two pid attributes so each is unambiguous. A real implementation can find matching pairs without materialising all nine, while preserving this meaning.

A natural join instead compares every same-named attribute and keeps one copy of each common attribute. Here it yields (pid,category,price) with (11,tea,20) and (13,cake,35). Adding a same-named column to both tables adds another equality test; with no shared names, natural join is a Cartesian product. Do not choose it merely because its syntax is shorter.

Renaming also gives one table two roles. For Employee(id,name,manager_id)={(1,An,2),(2,Binh,2)}, call one occurrence E and the other M. E.manager_id=M.id pairs An's row with Binh's row. E.id=M.id would pair An with himself. The rename changes names, not values or row count.

Try: add S(12,25). What changes before any price filter?

The product has 3×4=12 pairs; the equal-ID join gains (12,tea,12,25) and has three rows. The new price row cannot join with product 11 or 13 because the IDs differ.

Key takeaway

Projection in pure RA removes duplicate rows after selecting columns. R has no fully identical rows, but removing pid can make two rows identical. SQL SELECT category retains tea, tea, cake; SELECT DISTINCT category removes duplicates.

Does renaming Employee create different employee values?

No. E and M distinguish roles. E.manager_id=M.id matches employee to manager; renaming alone does not change rows.

sections.title: Move a filter only after explaining why it is safe
sections.html:
Return to the original R and S, without the added row. We want categories of products priced above 25. Compare two complete computations:

StageJoin firstFilter S first
First intermediateJoin: (11,tea,11,20), (13,cake,13,35)S with price>25: (13,35), (14,50)
Next intermediatePrice filter keeps product 13Join matches only product 13; R lacks 14
Project category{cake}{cake}

Write the left plan as π category(σ price>25(R ⋈ R.pid=S.pid S)). Write the right plan as π category(R ⋈ R.pid=S.pid σ price>25(S)). Read nested expressions from inside out. Both return cake, but the right plan never offers S's low-price row to the join. It may reduce work; it does not by itself prove a particular runtime improvement.

One dataset shows agreement only on that dataset. The reason the rewrite holds more generally is that price belongs entirely to S: if an S row fails price>25, pairing it with any R row cannot make it pass. We can discard it before this inner join. A condition involving R.category and S.price cannot generally move into S alone because S lacks category. Outer joins need different reasoning: preserving unmatched rows changes which transformations are safe.

The algebra describes logical transformations. A physical plan additionally chooses code such as a scan, an index lookup or a join algorithm. Optimisation may change both the logical arrangement and the physical methods, while preserving the specified result and its set or bag semantics. An efficient wrong answer is still wrong.

Try: can we project only category from R before joining on pid?

No. That projection removes pid, which the join still needs. Keep pid alongside category until the matching step is complete; only then may it be discarded.

Key takeaway

Push a condition only into an input containing every column it needs. If the condition needs both R and S, S alone lacks enough information to evaluate it. This argument applies to the example’s inner join; it must not be transferred unchanged to an outer join.

Can a predicate needing both R and S be pushed into S alone?

Not in general: S lacks the R values needed to evaluate it. The rewrite also needs its join-semantic assumptions.

sections.title: Count survivors, then count copies
sections.html:
Some questions combine whole sets rather than matching two columns. For A(x)={1,2,4} and B(x)={2,3}, examine each candidate value:

ValueIn A?In B?Union A∪BDifference A−BIntersection A∩B
1YesNoKeepKeepDrop
2YesYesKeepDropKeep
3NoYesKeepDropDrop
4YesNoKeepKeepDrop

Thus A∪B={1,2,3,4}, A−B={1,4}, A∩B={2}. Also A−(A−B) removes {1,4} from A, leaving {2}: intersection can be built from difference. Inputs need compatible schemas: same column count and corresponding types. UNION removes duplicate output rows in SQL; UNION ALL keeps copies.

Bag difference asks a second question: how many copies remain? If x occurs three times in A and once in B, subtract one occurrence from three, leaving max(3−1,0)=2 under EXCEPT ALL. Distinct EXCEPT removes x entirely because B contains it. SQLite lacks EXCEPT ALL; the Relational Lab demonstrates this bag operation separately.

An “every requirement” question goes further. Let Skill(person,skill)={(An,SQL),(An,RA),(Binh,SQL)} and Required(skill)={SQL,RA}. Candidate people come from Skill: An and Binh. An passes SQL and RA; Binh passes SQL but lacks RA. Division returns An. If Required is empty, every candidate in that projected person domain passes, because none has a missing requirement. This uses set values without SQL NULL.

Other extended vocabulary names tasks rather than magic new data: gamma groups and aggregates, delta eliminates bag duplicates, assignment names an intermediate value, and tau orders output. The slide deck mentions extensions; the division fixture here is original explanatory practice.

Try: add (Binh,RA), then add a new required skill Python without adding any Skill row. Who passes after each change?

First An and Binh both pass. After Python becomes required, neither passes: both lack that required pair. Having two skills is not the same as satisfying every member of the required set.

Which candidates satisfy division when Required is empty?

Every candidate in the projected Skill person domain, under the stated set-value semantics.

quiz.question: If R has 3 rows and S has 4 rows, how many rows does R × S contain?
quiz.explanation: Each R row combines with every S row: 3×4=12. The Cartesian product has not yet applied a join condition; a later selection may reduce the number of pairs.
